newsitem.title: UK: New EU draft gas directive too timid - UK's Battle.
newsitem.headline: New EU draft gas directive too timid - UK's Battle.

text.p: The European Union's new draft gas directive, published by the Luxembourg presidency earlier this week, does not go far enough in its proposals for competition, British energy minister John Battle said on Thursday.
"The text doesn't go as far as we'd like or as we believe is necessary for full competition," he said.
A new draft directive was published on July 22, a hearing of the House of Lords European Communities Committee's enquiry on the gas directive was told.

It differs from the previous draft in that it specifies the size of the market in each member state which must be opened to competition in the first tranche. Under the gas directive, Europe's markets are to be opened gradually, with users of more than a certain volume of gas allowed to purchase competitively. The size of these thresholds is to be gradually reduced.

The Luxembourg draft now says 28 percent of gas markets should be opened in the first wave. But the enquiry heard that this differs little from the previous proposal that users of over 25 million cubic metres a year should be able to buy competitively in the first wave, and will still only apply to "a handful" of large users.
Battle said the new 28 percent figure was close to Britain's wish to see a level of 30 percent. "But the tail of the phasing is nowhere near what the UK would like," he added.

Britain would like to see a section in the directive obliging gas companies to manage transport separately from their marketing and supply business, Battle said. This has already been done in Britain, where British Gas plc was demerged into BG plc which includes transport arm Transco, and the supply company Centrica plc.

And Battle also said Britain would like to see a faster and more ambitious programme for market opening, and a mandatory provision that pipeline companies should be made to expand their pipeline capacities to prevent bottlenecks in the future.
Asked how this could be done, Battle was not specific, but he added that "if it doesn't happen it blocks everything."

The minister also said that the new draft directive should effectively sort out the distinction between long-term take or pay contracts signed in the past and operational at present, and those to be signed in the future.

Take or pay contracts are one of the biggest sticking points in the directive. Many countries and companies have such contracts, popular with buyers as they appear to guarantee security of supply, and with sellers as the guarantee a market for their gas.

But they are regarded as anti-competitive, and the issue over how they should be resolved, or whether any should be subject to derogations or exemptions from the directive, is a stumbling block to the approval of the directive.

Battle was followed at the hearing by Erik Johnsen, Director General of the Norwegian ministry of petroleum and energy. Norway, which exports nearly all gas produced, is a keen advocate of take or pay contracts, and Johnsen supported them vigorously.

"Growth in (gas use in) Europe has been phenomenal. It will continue to grow at a healthy rate in the future. Take or pay contracts are an inherent part of the market. We don't think they're stifling growth, rather the opposite," he said.

Battle, by contrast, said categorically that "long term take or pay contracts are not essential to security of supply," and added that contracts covering much shorter periods could be just as effective.

But he was not disappointed with the text of the new draft, saying he welcomed it as a start but would like to see it go further. And the fact that the percentage size of the first tranche of the market to be opened was smaller than he thought appropriate was no discouragement, he said.
"The debate doesn't stop with this figure in this directive," he said, adding that the issue should be debated and kept alive in the European Parliament.
An energy council meeting will take place on December 8, he said, although there may be an exceptional meeting in October.
